subsubtopic: IMPACT OF LOW-LEVEL MILITARY TRAINING FLIGHTS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, this week a Gallup poll reports that 95 per cent of Canadians support more government funding for the protection of wilderness. Yet wilderness areas are coming under attack, not only from logging, mining and development, but from the air as well compliments of the Government of Canada.
Fighter planes already roar across Labrador at tree-top level. If the Department of National Defence gets its way and Goose Bay becomes a NATO training base, the number of overflights will increase substantially.
This year approval was given for B-52 and B-1B bombers to fly at less than 100 metres above ground over Lady Evelyn-Smoothwater Wilderness Park near Temagami in northern Ontario. The latest proposal is for bombers and fighter jets to practise over the skies of British Columbia starting in December.
The Government should respect Canadian passion for the wilderness and stop low-level military flights instead of permitting the militarization of Canadian wilderness.

Mr. Speaker, I was shocked, depressed and infuriated when I read in a book issued by the Department of the Secretary of State that there would be a new Oath of Allegiance for new citizens. I was horrified by the two options suggested: one, delegating the monarchy to
second place in the oath; and two, leaving the monarchy out altogether.
Why such an idea even appeared in a government booklet is incomprehensible. Surely when we take an Oath of Allegiance to Her Majesty, The Queen, we are pledging allegiance to Canada itself.
If the intention was to accommodate persons who want to become citizens of Canada and who object to taking our present Oath of Allegiance, they should go back to where they came from.
The monarchy stands for the highest and best principles of life and indeed binds our country with all other countries that form the great Commonwealth of Nations.
Every individual who takes our Oath of Allegiance by saying: "I do swear that I will be faithful and bear allegiance to Her Majesty Queen Elizabeth II" is following in the footsteps of thousands of Canadian soldiers, airmen and sailors who died for Canada in honouring that oath.
I commend the Secretary of State (Mr. Crombie) for saying yesterday in this Chamber: "It is not the Government's intention to withdraw Her Majesty from the Oath of Allegiance". Long live our Queen!

subsubtopic: FRANCHISE OUTLETS-APPLICATION OF CANADA LABOUR CODE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, Canadians got good news and bad news about Canada Post today. First, the good news. The Canadian Labour Relations Board decided unanimously that people working at postal franchise outlets must receive benefits and wages equal to those paid postal workers. This is a great victory for working Canadians and for Canada Post customers.
It is a victory for men and women in need of a living wage. It also means an end to cheap labour at franchise locations.
This is also a victory for the Canadian consumer. People in my riding, and Canadians from across the country, have been telling me that they want the Conservative Government to rethink the way it operates the Post Office. They want equality and uniformity of service for all Canadians whether they live in Thunder Bay, South Gillies, or Atikokan.
86%

September 2, 1987
Now for the bad news. Canada Post has finally decided that the mail is slow, something that Canadians have known for years, and only now does it want to find out why. The real rub is that it is going to take Canada Post three years to find out why the mail is slow.
This study already has proven why the mail is slow; incompetent management led by an incompetent Conservative Government.
There is a real solution to this problem and it starts with getting rid of the Conservative Government.

subsubtopic: RELEASE OF CONVICTED MURDERER TO CELEBRATE BIRTHDAY
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, another inmate is again being charged with at least one murder and perhaps more after being released on a temporary pass by the National Parole Board, for his birthday, believe it or not. Surely a birthday is insufficient reason for permitting a convicted killer to mingle with innocent Canadians at a mall, who err simply by being in the wrong place at the wrong time.
As we have recently, in a democratic, parliamentary vote, rejected the return of capital punishment, surely we as legislators must accept full responsibility for bringing in tougher parole laws to ensure a greater degree of safety for Canadians. I, for one, have no intention of reneging on my responsibility in this area. We continually hear of the rights of the accused and the guilty, but as I have stated many times in this House, I believe it is high time we concentrate on the collective rights and the protection of society as a whole.
When we reflect on the Sweeney case in which a convicted murderer was released on parole to kill viciously again, and then this recent case in Edmonton, is this not a clear message that it must not happen again? We must toughen the system and protect innocent Canadians.

Mrs. Lucie pepin (Outremont): Mr. Speaker, a good many men and women from Quebec and other Canadian communities are attending today's official opening of the Francophone Summit in the Quebec capital. This summit is a gathering of 40-odd state leaders and government heads whose common tie is the use of the French language.
Several themes are on the agenda. The participants will attempt to emphasize international policy and the world economic situation. Special consideration will be given to the poorer countries of the francophone community. Linked though they may be by the French language, these countries still carry a heavy burden.
As Governor General Sauve put it, what we are about to write is the history of francophones of the year 2000. Not only is it a matter of ensuring the continuity of the French language, but we must also promote dialogue among francophone countries. This is a major concern, and therefore political and economic co-operation has to be a foremost objective.
People of many countries have their eyes riveted on Quebec and Canada, and they closely follow the summit leaders to whom we extend our best wishes of success. Unfortunate though it may be, many of us Members of Parliament cannot attend the various events, but our hearts and minds are with the participants. We can only applaud and wish them good luck, hoping that this summit is a harbinger of many more such gatherings.

1988 MODEL AUTOMOBILES-NEW EMISSION CONTROL STANDARDS

Mr. Speaker, this month automobile manufacturers will be unveiling their 1988 models. These models will be required for the first time to comply with new emission standards aimed at significantly reducing the allowable emissions of nitrogen oxides from automobiles. These new emission standards, which came into effect yesterday, are another important step in the Government's fight against acid rain.
You will recall, Mr. Speaker, that in March, 1985, the Prime Minister (Mr. Mulroney) announced a national program to reduce acid rain to 50 per cent of its 1980 levels by 1994. That program included $150 million for emission controls at smelters, $25 million for technology development, $70 million for cleaner use of coal, $18 million per year for research and monitoring, efforts to increase the use of low sulphur western Canadian coal, and new automobile emission standards to go into effect September 1, 1987, for 1988 car models.
While half of our acid rain emissions comes from the United States, the other half originates in our own country. These new
automdbile emission standards will help us to get our own house in order.
CEREMONIES COfdMRMdRATING DIEPPE RAID

Mr. Speaker, recently a small group of Members from the House of Commons and the Senate accompahied the Minister of Veterans Affairs (Mr. Hees) and approximately 50 Dieppe veterans and officials from the Department of Veterans Affairs to the forty-fifth anniversary ceremonies commemorating the Dieppe Raid. We had many cenotaph remembrance events at cemeteries and battle sites during the course of the week.
I want to compliment the Minister of Veterans Affairs for the effective manner in which he conducted himself during the course of his official duties and for the sense of decency and the rapport with which he treated all of us in the delegation. The officials in the Department of Vetefflns Affairs deserve a big vote of congratulations on their organisation.
The number of Canadian graves that we visited in Britaih and in the Dieppe area of France tell the story of a terrible mission. Many other Canadian soldiers had to spend the war in captivity and, indeed, in a wounded state as a result of the raid. Our soldiers Were given an impossible mission on that dreadful morning of August 19, 1942. But there is no dispute whatsoever about the fact that the Canadians involved in the Dieppe Raid could not have done more.
One has only to attend remembrance ceremonies at the many cenotaphs in Europe to realize fully what a wealth of Canadian leadership is resting in the well-kept military cemeteries of Europe. One reads the names and the ages: 19 years old; 21 years old; 30 years old; 24 years old; and 18 years old. These young people never really had a chance to participate in the life of their own beloved nation, Canada.
In the Act of Remembrance we state that: "We will remember them". But do we really remember them? Do we in this House of Commons fully realize that we are here because of them? Every day must be a remembrance day for such gallant Canadians and, indeed, for us. We have had the torch of freedom and responsibility passed to us to handle difficult problems in this country and in the world at large. How well we handle these challenges will be a reflection of how well we will remember them.

Hear, hear!

September 2, 1987

subtopic: PUBLICATION ON FUTURE USE OF HYDROGEN
PUBLICATION ON FUTURE USE OF HYDROGEN
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I wish to draw to the attention of Parliament the recently published report of the Advisory Group on Hydrogen Opportunities chaired by Professor David Scott of the University of Toronto. The report is entitled Hydrogen-National Mission for Canada. The establishment of such a mission is its principal recommendation.
In the future it is likely that electricity and hydrogen, readily interchangeable, will be the forms or sources of energy in most common use. We are fortunate that these are largely non-polluting.
With its resources of natural gas for steam reforming and hydroelectricity for electrolysis, plus our brain power in industry and in universities, Canada stands poised to reap the opportunities in this new and exciting field. The positive reception of this report by the Government augurs well for the future of hydrogen technology in Canada.

subtopic: AWARDING OF CONTRACTS IN BRITISH COLUMBIA
AWARDING OF CONTRACTS IN BRITISH COLUMBIA
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, British Columbians and British Columbia firms for many years have been anxious and keen to do business with the Canadian International Development Agency. British Columbians have the interest, the expertise, the skills and the experience to offer their services, goods and equipment to CIDA for Canadian overseas development projects. However, British Columbians have been and still are shut out of doing CIDA work.
While the Liberals were in office although British Columbia had 35 per cent of Ontario's population it received only 14 per cent of the number of contracts received by Ontario. However, under the Tories the situation has actually worsened with B.C. now receiving only 12 per cent of the number of contracts received by Ontario, and worth only 11 per cent of the value.
1 urge the Progressive Conservative Government to have more faith in British Columbians and in British Columbia, to show an interest and to take initiatives to recognize British Columbian talent, expertise, experience and ability when it comes to filling CIDA contracts.
British Columbians ask not for any extraordinary consideration-only that they receive their fair share of CIDA service contracts, goods and equipment contracts and industrial cooperation contracts. British Columbians do not expect special treatment, only justice and fairness.

subtopic: MEMBER FOR SKEENA'S REPORTED REFERENCE TO NOVA SCOTIANS

speakeroldname: Mr. Lawrence I. O'Neil (Cape Breton Highlands-Canso):
subtopic: MEMBER FOR SKEENA'S REPORTED REFERENCE TO NOVA SCOTIANS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, yesterday Canadians heard an amazing admission from the Hon. Member for Skeena (Mr. Fulton). He told us that he is closer to the people of Central and South America than to many other Canadians. He referred to countries in that region of the world as sister countries. He singled out Nova Scotians as a group to which he is not close. He did not call Nova Scotia a sister province. What must Nova Scotia do to become a sister province-elect a socialist government?
For whom does the Hon. Member speak? Is he representing the views of British Columbians when he says that they have a closer relationship to Central America than to Atlantic Canada? I do not think so. I am sure that my sister and my brother living in B.C. do not agree. I can assure Hon. Members that he is not speaking for Nova Scotians.
The Hon. Member's admission reflects his personal emotions. When he says that Central America has a closer relationship to B.C. than Nova Scotia he represents only the world as he sees it. It is a shameful comment on his Party's feelings for Atlantic Canadians and for our country-the greatest country in the world.
I ask the Hon. Member to stand in his place and apologize to his constituents for this gross misrepresentation of their loyalties, and for this slight to all Nova Scotians that he purports to offer on their behalf.

Mr. Speaker, recently the Russell County Milk Committee wrote a letter to the excellent Premier of Ontario, Mr. David Peterson. In the letter they state:
The Russell County Milk Committee is quite concerned about the "free trade" and the impact it could do to the dairy industry.
Everybody knows we have the best supply management in the world and it should not be traded away in whole or in part. There is no doubt it cannot be compared with the American system. It costs a lot less for the taxpayers to support a system like ours than what they have in the States, plus the fact that our financial stability is entirely due to our system.
The letter concludes by stating:
September 2, 1987

We have had a lot of pressure from concerned dairymen in the last months over the free trade issue, and we hope that your Government will keep an eye on our federal counterparts concerning this matter.
Yours truly,
Leo Brisson,
Russell County Milk Committee.
It is obvious that the Russell County Milk Committee is very concerned about the fact that the Government in Ottawa could trade away supply management, and it is counting on the excellent Liberal Government of Ontario to defend it, as does the excellent Liberal Party in Ottawa.

Mr. Speaker, I wish to urge the Minister of State for Privatization (Mrs. McDougall) to privatize Petro-Canada. But I wish it to be done in a unique, innovative manner, and not let it slip into foreign hands. I want to give Petro-Canada to the 25 million citizens of Canada.
My plan is deceptively simple. Every man, woman, and child would be given a proportionate share of the common shares owned by the federal Government. Canadians would be given first rights to future share issues.
1 believe the Government has an obligation to ensure security of supply of oil and gas resources by ensuring that they are developed on a timely basis. I do not believe this means being in the retail gasoline station business.
Governments should only intrude in the market-place if it serves a public policy objective. In my wildest imagination, I cannot imagine how government ownership of retail gasoline pumps meets a public policy objective.
Let us give the shares of this corporation to the people of Canada. In a sense they already own it because Governments have poured hundreds of millions of taxpayers' dollars into this organization, and provided it with enormous tax concessions. Petro-Canada has been quick to raise prices at the pump when crude oil prices rise, but it is not so quick to drop prices when crude oil prices decline.
Who knows, we may even create a healthier, more competitive market-place with Canadians in charge, and keep control in this country.
Oral Questions

Mr. Speaker, after nearly three years in office this Conservative Government-ever mindful of its unbelievably stupid blunders concerning elderly Canadians, such as de-indexation of old age security pensions, unemployment insurance discrimination towards older workers, cut-backs of about $5 million in the New Horizons program-this Government, as 1 said, has decided to buy off elderly Canadians by appointing a Minister of State for Senior Citizens.
Mr. Speaker, a better man could not have been chosen for this job, but we want to be sure that the Government considers the well-being of senior citizens as something more than a smokescreen and window-dressing. Therefore I would urge the Minister responsible for Senior Citizens to eliminate discrimination with respect to the spouse's allowance, single, separated or divorced women, to cancel the New Horizons $5 million cut-back, and to correct the situation concerning the unfair treatment meted out to older workers seeking unemployment insurance benefits. Then people will have faith in this Government.

speakeroldname: Hon. Benoit Bouchard (Minister of Employment and Immigration) moved
speechtext:
that Bill C-84, an Act to amend the Immigration Act, 1976 and the Criminal Code in consequence thereof, be read the third time and passed.
He said: Mr. Speaker, I fully appreciate this opportunity to thank the Members of the legislative committee on Bill C-84 who, I think, worked long hours on this legislative measure. I would also like to thank the people, groups or individuals, who commented on this Bill.

As we all know, Canada's refugee determination system is under siege against a daily onslaught of illegal migrants arriving in Canada and making false claims to gain entrance. The number of claims in 1987 is expected to be some 30,000. Refugee determination is a complex and often emotional issue. The question of abuse and how to eliminate it is crucial to preserving Canada's humanitarian reputation and our tradition for law and order. That is why the Parliament of Canada was recalled in the middle of August. I repeat, Mr. Speaker, that I believe that was more than useful in order to take immediate, decisive action to put an end to the growing, flagrant abuse of our laws and generosity.

Over the past few weeks, Mr. Speaker, we have heard the views of a number of interest groups and individuals on the best way to correct the flaws they thought they had spotted in the Bill. I listened closely to their suggestions and concerns, and I take this opportunity to comment briefly on the amendments proposed by the legislative committee.
Mr. Speaker, I think it bears repeating that from the outset I gave Canadians and committee Members the assurance that I would consider the possibility of amending the Bill, on the condition that this would not weaken it in any way. I feel that the amendments endorsed by the House are useful and necessary explanations, and I support them unreservedly.
The Bill is aimed at severely cracking down on the operations of unscrupulous counsellors, smugglers who take advantage of the plight of illegal migrants, and carriers who fail to ensure, as they should, that their passengers carry the required documents. It is also aimed at curbing abuses on the part of economic migrants who try to jump ahead of refugees and immigrants who abide by the established procedure.
Mr. Speaker, proposed Sections 95.1 and 95.2 are the key provisions of these legislative measures, enabling us as they will to put a stop to the activities of those who bring many illegal migrants into Canada.

There has been much discussion about amending these articles. We have insisted that lawyers and legal drafters consider different phrases. We have considered terms such as religious group, profit, reward, fraud and clandestine entry, but each option creates loopholes and reduces our capacity to prosecute the unscrupulous. The bottom line of this legislation, Mr. Speaker, is that we cannot permit these individuals to escape sanction by creating insurmountable problems of proof.
I reject the argument that proposed Sections 95.1 and 95.2 open doors to prosecution which were not open before. The current Act had this general offence but it did not serve as a deterrent to Captain Nygren. Through proposed Sections 95.1 and 95.2, we bring it forward as a clearly marked and highlighted offence with higher penalties.
There has been a great deal of talk about how this Bill would affect church groups. I would like to respond to these concerns. It has been said that because we have two new proposed Sections, we have opened up the door to the prosecution of church and humanitarian groups if they assist refugees. I reject this. Since 1976 there have been penalties in the Act for any person who brings undocumented people into Canada. Therefore, church groups have been liable to prosecution for the past 10 years. There have been no complaints before and, to my knowledge, no prosecutions. The reason is that the administration of this Act has always recognized and will continue to recognize the humanitarian nature of these activities.
What was true before is true now under the current legislation and under the new Bill. Bill C-84 does not create some new ground of prosecution for what church and humanitarian groups have been doing for years, presenting refugee claimants for examination, sponsoring refugees from abroad and providing settlement assistance.
Proposed Sections 95.1 and 95.2 address both the enormity and the immediacy of the situation. They send strong signals that Canada will no longer tolerate abuse of our borders and our laws. The message is clear and the audience is specific. Those who seek to ignore or circumvent our laws will be prosecuted. It is as simple as that.

In connection with Clause 8, Mr. Speaker, I should like to stress that proposed Section 103.1 of the Bill empowers the Minister either to order a ship captain to sail into port or to send him back. This amendment, proposed by the Hon. Member for Calgary North (Mr. Gagnon), confirms the assurance I gave the High Commissioner for Refugees, Mr. Hocke, that the Government has every intention of exercising its power to send ships back, but without endangering human lives nor breaching the Geneva Convention.
September 2, 1987

I am sure the House will agree that the amendment proposed by the Hon. Member for Willowdale (Mr. Oostrom) to add a new proposed section, 95.4, will make it easier for us to take legal action against unscrupulous counsellors who urge refugee status claimants to make false statements. This amendment provides for stiffer penalties for this kind of infraction.
The House has accepted two other technical amendments which clarify the Bill.

To conclude, this Bill is designed to meet an urgent situation. It has been drafted to hit hard at a new type of criminal activity, namely, large scale smuggling. It also strengthens our ability to quickly remove criminal and security risks. It will allow us as well to slow down, and perhaps put an end to the increasing flood of people arriving in Canada without travel documents.
This legislation, together with Bill C-55, will provide a comprehensive, long-term solution to the difficulties and abuses currently surrounding the refugee determination process. It will enable us to concentrate on helping those refugees truly in need of our protection. It will enable us to continue our strategy of controlled growth in immigration.

Mr. Speaker, I am convinced that this legislation is essential if we are to respect our humanitarian commitment towards refugees in the world and to prevent possible frauds against Canadians or Canadian laws. Bill C-84 will enable this country to do that.

Mr. Speaker, on behalf of my Party 1 am pleased to respond as the lead-off speaker in the final phase, in the House of Commons at any rate, of this Bill, namely third reading. The Bill received interesting treatment at second reading when Hon. Members actively participated. We have just come from very active deliberations in the legislative committee.
I regret that the attitude of the Minister is the same. It is the same inflexible position that was the position of the Government at second reading. It is the same inflexible position that was displayed during the study of Bill C-84 in legislative committee. It is the same inflexible position that was reflected in the clause-by-clause study of the Bill. Witness after witness came to Ottawa on short notice and prepared to help the Parliament of Canada in its deliberations to try to ensure a better, more fair and more effective Bill. Despite that the inflexibility persists. In the short 10 to 15 minutes that the Minister took in his speech on third reading the same inflexibility persisted. It rang out loud and clear. That is unfortunate because the issue is so sensitive.
In saying that I do not mean to suggest that any issue with which we deal in the House of Commons takes priority or second place to other issues. But certainly when we talk about
Immigration Act, 1976
immigration we must recognize the sensitivity and, beyond that, I believe the emotions that are attached to immigration policy.
I have spent only three years in this.Chamber. Like every other Member of Parliament, when I go back to my riding I keep constituency appointments with people who live in my riding. Their problems range from trying to find employment, to trying to find a summer job, to an individual who cannot pay his tuition, to an individual who wants to collect Canada Pension Plan disability benefits because of an injury received on a construction site. All those issues are important. They mean the world to the individuals who bring them forward. However, with respect to immigration-related problems there is no doubt that the emotional level attached to them poses the most serious dilemma and problems for us as Members of Parliament.
When we talk about immigration outside of the refugee flow and the refugee program we are talking about people in Canada, Canadians who wish their families to join them, who want visitors to visit them, who want their cousins to attend the University of Toronto to obtain an education on a visitor's visa. We have all sorts of requests. It is emotionally difficult for persons to understand why their mothers, their grandmothers, their aunts, their cousins, their nephews or their friends were refused by the Department, by the bureaucracy. It becomes difficult because we are talking about human feelings and about human beings. That is why I thought that there could have been some movement, some sensitivity displayed by the Government of Canada in terms of responding to those, at many times, emotional pleas from a wide range of groups.
We heard from the Inter-Church Committee, from the clergy, from the Canadian Bar Association which gave a legal perspective, and from civil libertarians. We heard from Canadians who came on short notice to give a bit of themselves to the input and the drafting of this legislation. I am left to ask myself this question. Are we any richer for it as a Parliament if we continue, as the Government does, simply to play the charade, to pass the legislation in a vacuum, to explain it to one's caucus on a Wednesday morning as if nothing else mattered outside that room or on the drafting board in the Minister's office? We cannot continue to draft legislation in that sense.
While the purpose and objective of this legislation is certainly noble for everyone in the House, it is the process that has to be paid some respect and some regard since it is the process that has a way of affecting the substance. In this case there was little process. There was no respect given to the witnesses or to the testimony given during the process. As a result we have a piece of legislation which I believe is made poorer as a result of that indifference and intransigence. That is why at the eleventh hour of third reading there was still a trickle of hope that the Minister could have moved a number of amendments on a number of grounds.

On behalf of my Party I moved close to 20 amendments, not in an attempt to scuttle Bill C-84 or to suggest that the Liberal Party does not wish to clamp down on abuse. All Members in all Parties wish to clamp down on abuse. It was a way of achieving that without sacrificing many of the principles that I will be deliberating and outlining for the House.
My colleague, the Hon. Member for Spadina (Mr. Heap), on behalf of his Party, presented a large number of amendments to improve and precisely target the objectives of Bill C-84. At different times, Members of the Minister's Government made various remarks or suggestions which reflected that perhaps there could be some movement. Yet, we are at third reading, and the Minister has articulated the same position today as he did at first and second readings.
If that was the intention of the Government, and it knew what it would say at third reading today, then I think it could have avoided putting Canadians, Members, research staff, and everyone else through the hoop; through a process that, in the end, counted for absolutely nothing.
The substance of the Bill is worrisome, but also the process taken by the Government is equally alarming. Today it is Bill C-84, tomorrow perhaps it will be Bill C-55 which may be treated in the same manner, and other Bills down the line. Therefore, we move away from participatory democracy because there is no public participation or involvement, and no accommodation of the input from the public. There is no respect for the opinion of anyone other than the Minister.
That is not the openness and the accessible Government preached by the Prime Minister (Mr. Mulroney) in 1983 or 1984 when he was campaigning, visiting various towns and hamlets, and visiting the church basements which I do not think he will dare to step in after Bill C-84.

Canadians should not continuously be talked to and dictated to; they should participate with the Government in improving its legislation in order that the laws created and administered, if not agreed with, will be respected by Canadians.
The committee heard testimony from many people who suggested that they have no respect for the legislation, especially in the literal sense, in terms of those individuals who would now be liable to fines or imprisonment for assisting refugees who may not have visas. Those individuals have said that they will continue to pursue their legitimate work in assisting refugees.
Therefore, I ask the Minister, what is the purpose of drafting legislation which is not rooted and grounded with
some degree of moral respectability from citizens? The process has been alarming and discouraging.
We talk about parliamentary reform and suggest that committees will have more political power and greater input; committees will be allowed to question the Minister on the laws, provide a check and balance, and make a Member of Parliament feel like a somebody. That is not evident in Bill C-84. Thus far it is not evident in Bill C-55. Four witnesses were jammed into a morning session which lasted two hours. What committee deals with four different witnesses, assuming that there will be two rounds of questioning from Members at the table? If we allow other legislation to be properly scrutinized, why should immigration Bills be the exception? Why should Bills C-84 and C-55 set a wrong and dangerous precedent? These questions of process impact in a very real manner on the substance that we are debating.
In terms of dealing with the substance, I would like to begin with a short quote from Rabbi Gunther Plaut. I do not suggest that his testimony was any better than any other witness, but it was an inspirational speech that he delivered to the legislative committee. He even impressed and touched Members on the government side, judging from the attention, the questions, and the duration of his speech, and from the compliments of the government chairman. Rabbi Plaut touched a nerve that day, and one would have thought his testimony would have moved the Government to realize that amendments in certain clauses were correct and necessary if we were to maintain the sense of justice that has prevailed in Canada.
At the beginning of his testimony to the legislative committee he stated:
You can render the Canadian people and the refugee community of the
world and causes of humanity in general a true service if you manage to
eliminate from this Bill clauses that treat such people worse than the worst of
criminals.
Rabbi Plaut further stated:
Treat the stranger fairly; you should extend your love and friendship to him.
Remember that you too were strangers once.
That last line which addresses the stranger among us left a five-second interval of silence at the committee. In fact, the stranger among us represents the history and the roots of this country.
We can engage in a numbers game as to how many people were born here, how many people immigrated here, how many are the sons and daughters of immigrants but born here; the numbers can be debated, but perhaps no agreement will be reached as to how many individuals constitute second, and third generations of Canadians of immigrant families.
Over-all it cannot be denied that in large measure this country was built by the impressive flows of immigrants to our shores. In a real and conscious way, Canada opened its doors to the world, invited and welcomed people to begin a new life, take a new lease on life and start anew in Canada. In the process of offering those individuals a new opportunity and a new life, we were breathing life into Canada and building a

new, bigger, and better country. That is the role that immigration has played in this country. It is a national building block. It has been in the past, it continues to be in the present, and it will be so in the future.
It is important to have that perspective when dealing with this emergency legislation, and to give some thought as to what are the future implications for our immigration program overall, specifically with respect to refugees.
I think everybody would agree and recognize the reality that immigration played a tremendously large and significant role, particularly in the post-Second World War era. We also must recognize that immigration will play the same type of role in the future. We only need to look at the statistics and the realities of our country in 1987. There is a dwindling birth rate, and families are having fewer children compared to 15 or 20 years ago. That will have a very serious impact on population trends, as well as social and economic implications.
At the same time we have an aging population. As a percentage of our population we have many more older Canadians than 10 or 15 years ago. It is not difficult to see the economic and social implications for Canada as a result of those two trends.
As well, every single year 50,000 more people leave our country than return. That has been the trend. Combine all those facts with the physical size of this country and I think the results are very clear.
Then we have our economic needs. Obviously immigration has to be matched with the country's ability to absorb immigrants; that is, to employ people and produce the goods and services so that everyone can enjoy their share. Those economic needs are continually changing, yet our education system does not necessarily adapt to those changes. We have to ensure that we have people with the skills necessary to meet Canada's requirements.
One of the best examples I can give is one close to home. My father is a tool and die maker with a small shop. He produces the tools and dies that go into punch presses which in turn produce all sorts of goods. Yet when my father requires tool and die makers he cannot find them. We have to go to Great Britain to obtain people with expertise in tool and die making. I ask myself why. Immigration offers an answer.
Immigration can help build this country and bring about greater economic prosperity. If that is true, and I happen to believe it is, then you would think this House, together with Canadians, could have a mature and rational debate on the process we are talking about today. What role does immigration play? What kind of immigration do we want to initiate? How many people can we absorb? What kind of trades do we need which our education system lags behind in producing? What are the goals we wish to set for ourselves?

You get the impression from the Government that immigration is something that you somehow have to tolerate. I think that is the wrong approach. It should be a pro-active, positive approach which utilizes immigration as a tool-not over the short term, as we are doing now, but articulating a vision of things to come-a vision which is consistent, progressive, and tells the world we know what we want in the way of immigration policy. We should be able to say that for the next 10, 15 or 20 years this is our agenda. It would be subject to some changes, of course, here and there, but we would not be opening the doors today, closing them tomorrow, and opening them a bit the next day. That does not work to the benefit of Canada.
Defining immigration policy is not easy. It is a very complex part of government policy. It is a large and very sensitive program. Do Canadians want to open up family class reunification? That has been a cornerstone of immigration policy for a good many years. Do we wish to assist the brothers and sisters of Canadians, for example, in immigrating by providing them with a higher priority? Do we wish to offer more points to those with family in this country? I think most Canadians would agree that the family has a role to play.
The arguments of the detractors of immigration would perhaps be blunted if we suggest that if they are worried that the state is going to spend too much on immigrants, do not worry because we are encouraging more family related immigration and the family will take care of the immigrant, thank you very much, and do a much better job.
How many visitors do we want in Canada? Should we have visitors' visas? Should we have a limit on the number of people who can come to Canada, the length of time they can stay, and where they come from? Should we allow more student visas? Should we allow more foreign students to come to Canada? Some people ask, if we allow too many foreign students what happens to our students? People may be worried that students from some corner of the world will do better than their little Johnny. Is that fair? Does their little Johnny lose a place at university if we have too many foreign students?
Other people suggest that once these students obtain their degrees and go back to their own countries they become goodwill ambassadors for Canada. If a student from Hong Kong studies at the University of Toronto for four years, goes back and works for an international computer company, do you not think that he will have a good understanding of this country? It could be that that individual will make a trip here in his capacity as marketing manager for the Hong Kong computer company. How many jobs would that create? How much wealth will that bring in to Canada?
Do we allow more immigrants to come in on temporary work permits? A construction firm in my riding went to the employment centre and asked for some bricklayers and carpenters. A couple of months went by and no one could fill the bill. Then he went to Immigration Canada. He said since the employment centre did not send him any workers he

But there is merit in intellectual stimulation, in trying to use practical examples to create practical policies that work for Canadians. Do we want to encourage more independent immigrants, people who do not have family here but who have good professions? Do we penalize independents too harshly if they do not have family? Do we encourage more entrepreneurs, more business immigration? This Government has doubled the number of business immigrants. Some people say that is bad and other people say that is positive. Others say that business immigrants bring wealth into the country, they create jobs, build new shops and factories, while others say this approach is that of buying your way into the country. This country was also built by individuals who came here with very little in their financial pockets, but a lot upstairs, with will and determination.
What is the absorption rate of entrepreneurs? What is the philosophical argument about whether a person with $200,000 can get into Canada without perhaps showing the right guarantees that a factory will be built or that he will create the number of jobs purported? Should we perhaps base our policy more on accepting individuals who wish to come here and give of themselves, stay permanently, and so on?
What about domestic work? What numbers of domestic helpers should we have? We have a program just to deal with domestic help. From where should they come and how many? Should we perhaps try to encourage domestic help in Canada before going abroad to get people? Once those people are here, what kind of opportunities or rights do they have? Why can't they stay a little longer if they manage to have a family in Canada and want to put roots down here? What is the implication of the program?
Then we have refugees. How many refugees shall we allow into Canada and from where? How do we select them? Should we go only in the refugee camps? Should we have a system in place that allows a person who comes to our borders due process, so that he or she can be accepted? Do we not have the obligation to follow a number of refugees through the system to see where they end up five or ten years hence?
It is troubling, but we seem to be hearing from different quarters that the word refugee has become a dirty word all of a sudden, that refugees are queue-jumpers and abusers. Those are the sort of reactionary comments we hear. We have to
define what is the true story of the refugee phenomenon in this country.
What about the Gunther Plaut who came to our committee? Gunther Plaut was a refugee himself, a lawyer and a rabbi. He is intelligent, moving and forceful. He sat on the committee with all of the other Members of Parliament who were not refugees. Not only did he hold his own, he went far beyond what the Members could in that room.
What is the reality and what is it that frightens us? Is that fear legitimate or is it perception? If it is a perception, how do we dispel the perception? That is what I mean when I say we have to define a vision of things to come. We have to do it maturely, in a vigorous and positive way. That is a responsibility of Government, but not exclusively. It is the responsibility of the communities, the churches and the non-profit organizations to be concerned and to reach out. By and large the ultimate decision must be that of the Government elected by Canadians.
In terms of performance; in educating, leading, inspiring, eliciting confidence, putting trust in an immigration policy that works, the Government's report card shows failure. 1 do not say that because I sit on this side of the House and the Government is on that side. I do not recall, but I urge Government Members to think of a time when a government of Canada, regardless of its political stripes, Conservative or Liberal, mismanaged the immigration policy as badly as we have seen in the last three years. This Government's policy has wreaked confusion in the minds of individuals. We have seen a policy under which family class reunification has lower priority while business class immigration has a higher one. There is confusion about the lack of clarity in our refugee policy. 1 think of those individuals in this country who have no business being here at all, and about the individuals with criminal backgrounds who have been getting special permits, compared to other individuals who were being left out. I have never seen, in three years, such a lack of confidence in an immigration policy. If you can ask you will find that most Canadians are confused about the direction the Government wants to set for itself in immigration policy. Beyond that confusion, there has been confusion purposely allowed to fester between what is an immigrant and what is a refugee. That is the second type of confusion. The first one is over-all, the second is very precise.
For the last three years this House, the Standing Committee on Employment, Labour and Immigration, and non-governmental organizations have said one thing very clearly. If we are going to make strides in refugee policy we have to delineate between who is a refugee and who is an immigrant. But that has not been done, Mr. Speaker. What have we had is the Prime Minister saying all of a sudden, when this boatload arrived, as reported in a Canadian Press article of July 31, 1987:
These people by and large are illegal aliens. They are people jumping the queue and taking the place of other immigrants.

That is false. The Minister knows that is false. The Members who serve on the committee with me know that is false. An individual refugee does not take the place of an immigrant. If my cousin from Country x cannot come in, it is not because we have accepted two or 200 refugees but because the targets have either been met or the individual does not, for a wide range of reasons, come within the immigration class, but he is not refused because of any refugee being accepted or refused. That confusion is being manipulated.
One of the greatest frustrations Canadians experience is the sponsoring of family and friends. People cannot understand why a relative, who would be given room and board and a job, with financial responsibility for his or her shortcomings, cannot come to Canada. The Government has allowed to fester and has manipulated that frustration. We hear that persons cannot enter because we have so many refugees queue jumping. That was the word used by the Prime Minister. That is not fair. It is not right because there are two streams, one for immigrants and one for legitimate refugees.
Legitimate immigration applicants apply at embassies abroad, state their reasons for applying, get medical and security checks and an answer is provided. That answer is yes, no or conditional. The reality is that a true, legitimate refugee who is facing persecution, torture, imprisonment, loss of liberty or probable death does not have the luxury to line up for a visa or to get proper documentation. The only luxury that person has is the luxury of some time to remove himself and his family from his country.
We are all proud of our birthplaces. Given the opportunity and the choice, no one in his right mind would want to be an immigrant. Immigration is motivated by either poverty, war, lack of a job, lack of a future or a revolution. Under those circumstances people pack their bags and move. However, given the choice, they would rather enjoy the fruits of their efforts in their own countries. When they cannot, they move for the betterment of their families and themselves. They adopt a new country to which they are loyal and patriotic. That is the reality of immigration. Given a choice, my family would have preferred to remain in northeastern Italy but there was nothing there for them at that time. Times have changed, but my parents are now Canadians. They would not trade Canada for any other including their homeland, as much as they still feel emotions for it. As much as they feel a tingle when they get off the airplane in their homeland, they feel a tingle on the return trip to Canada as well.
Given an ideal world, there would be no immigrants. However, we do not live in that ideal world. In addition, true refugees do not even have the option of trying to weather the storms in their countries. They have to leave; some of them come to Canada, some go to the United States and others go to Europe.

We must admit to ourselves that it is intellectually dishonest to confuse immigrants with refugees and to suggest that refugees block other immigrants. They do not. We do not even reach our immigration targets. The Minister has said that there is a target of 115,000 for landed immigrants but the Department always falls short by 10,000, 15,000 or 20,000. There are not enough people working in our embassies abroad to process these immigrants. Targets go up but the number of workers in visa offices stay the same. Unless those people work 24 hours a day, they will not process any more. One cannot draw blood from a stone. Therefore, it is very dishonest to base policies on those kinds of manipulations.
When I say that this is the worst performance I have ever seen, I do not mean to say that other Conservative Governments have the same record. I say that this Conservative administration, whether intentionally, whether because there has been a series of different Ministers with different goals or whether it is the Prime Minister, has given one of the worst performances I have seen.
Compare its performance, for instance, to that of the Government of 1979 led by the Right Hon. Member for Yellowhead (Mr. Clark), followed after nine months by the Trudeau Government. The best example I can offer to show the dichotomy between the two administrations is the example of the boat people.
Within a three-year period, Canada accepted 106,000 Vietnamese boat people. Approximately half of these were sponsored by the Government and half sponsored by communities, Members of this Chamber, parish priests, local community groups and local ratepayers who found families who would take in a number of young Vietnamese children. The acceptance of that 106,000 in three years was begun by the Government of the Right Hon. Member for Yellowhead, and finished by Mr. Trudeau's Government. That is leadership.
How was that accomplished? It was not accomplished through irrational thought. It was not accomplished by wondering what we would do with the boatloads of people who were coming. No, the Government clearly articulated for the nation the need to help these individuals. Other places in the world did the same. There was education. There was integration and acceptance by Canadians. Canadians demonstrated confidence that the Government would accomplish it in an orderly way. Canadians felt that these people really were refugees and we could absorb them into the community without there being an over-indulgence in the social welfare system if the Government would pay all the costs. All those barriers were taken into account and what was the result? The result was that Canadians moved progressively, sensibly and calmly. That is but one example of many in history.
There have been special refugee movements of people numbering in the thousands. After the Czechoslovakian revolution, there were 37,000 refugees. Again, through education, integration and a sense of balance, purpose and

Those studies show that those refugees from Vietnam, who are loyal and proud Canadians today, have done very well. Many of them have opened up their own businesses and shops. Others are happy working, making a dollar. Their kids have done very well in the educational system. They are producing and contributing citizens, just like you and I, Mr. Speaker. If we see them walking down the street-we cannot call them refugees, given the stigma we have allowed the word "refugee" to take on in the last couple of months.
The Canadians who accepted the Vietnamese boat people in the late 1970s and early 1980s are the same Canadians who live here today. It is not a different population. It is not as if the Canadians who were here in the late 1970s and the early 1980s all left and were replaced with another set of Canadians who all of a sudden have a different vision of immigration. They are the same people. Canada is the same country. It is only four years after the fact. If the people are the same, why-then are we getting such a drastically different reaction from the Government? Why is it an emergency when 300 people arrive in two boats over two summers? That is 300 compared to 106,000 in one special refugee flow. It is not acceptable for the Government to react in the way it did to those 300. We have a much prouder history than that.
I am not suggesting that we should not have orderly systems or should reward abuse. The checks and balances must be in place. If there are people who are illegitimately here and persist in circumventing the laws they should be deported instantly. I support that as do all Canadians.
We are here discussing an approach, evolving with the times and taking a humanitarian and responsible role. I find it unacceptable, with our history, that the Government, its Ministers and the Prime Minister should react in the fashion in which they have reacted.
The Canadian Ethnocultural Council, an organization representing national ethnic groups across the country, presented a very thoughtful brief entitled, "Reason over Hysteria, Please". That title captures the essence of this very well. We have always been guided by moderation, reason, thoughtfulness and a sense of progressivity.
Ministers of the Crown and Members of Parliament are suggesting that Canada is the only country to which refugees are coming, that somehow Canada is a sucker for refugees. I do not mean to use that word impolitely, but that is what I hear on the streets. It is the responsibility of the Government
to say that that is not true. The refugee movement is a world phenomenon.
Refugees are produced by uprisings, revolutions, dictatorships and war. When we listen to the national news in the evening and read the papers in the morning we learn about refugee uprisings, protests for peace and democracy, people put in prison, people killed and people tortured. We are bombarded with that. The world is in turmoil and is producing refugees as we speak.
The existence of refugees presents a world-wide problem which needs a world-wide solution. A domestic solution within Canada will do nothing to help the problem in the world. West Germany, Canada, Switzerland, the United States, Brazil and other countries must come together in a mood of co-operation to try and resolve the problem collectively. That is why we signed the Geneva Convention in the 1950s.
What is the Geneva Convention? When you strip away the technical and fancy words which Canadians may not understand, the Geneva Convention is a fancy way of saying that we are all besieged with the problem and in order to solve it we must all act in unison. That is why we signed the pact.
The agreement says, first, that we must be proactive, meaning that we have a responsibility to go to the various refugee camps in the world. I have had the opportunity of visiting some of them. It is not a pleasant sight to see a refugee camp surrounded by barbed wire. People live within those camps for five or six years, have children there, and are not able to leave. Countries within the pact send visa officers to refugee camps to select refugees to bring to their countries in hopes of diminishing the numbers of people in the camps.
In addition to being proactive we agreed to be reactive. We agreed not to send people back to their homeland who, upon their return, will face persecution, torture or death. Those are the two things to which we as a country agreed under the Geneva Convention. That is what the Government should be explaining. The Government should be honouring that agreement rather than breaking it.
The Government should be explaining the transition in the plight of refugees. There are a number of Members and Ministers who say that this is the fault of the Liberal Government, that we are in a mess in 1987 because of the policies of Pierre Elliott Trudeau or the inaction of the previous administration. I do not say this because I sit on this side of the House, Mr. Speaker, but that is incorrect. The previous Government recognized that a transition was taking place. No longer were the majority of people waiting in the refugee camps. They were trying to get away from the camps, reach other countries, and ask for status. We did not have a system in place to handle such a large number of applicants coming to our shores.
When the previous administration saw the trickle of people arriving in Canada it tried to put in place a new structure. That is why it commissioned Rabbi Gunther Plaut to do a study and recommend a new system by which we could handle

The Government seems to be promoting its policy on the basis of curbing abuse. While the Government may suggest that it has a monopoly on the stand against abuse, I believe that no one in the House welcomes abuse, encourages it, or wishes to reward those who manipulate and circumvent our laws by smuggling, trafficking and trading in human lives.
Unfortunately, abuse exists in other areas of government responsibility. There are people who abuse unemployment insurance, the pension system, and the worker's compensation claims system. No one likes abuse, but, as in every other society, abuse sometimes permeates the very best system that a country and government can offer. The Government should be vigilant in attempting to stamp out abuse, as we have done in the Opposition. We did not sit quietly during the schemes and scams from Portugal, Turkey and Brazil, where individuals were selling visas and passports, counselling people to come here and make fraudulent claims based on religious persecutions that did not exist.
Why has the Government not acted? Why have people not been charged as a result of RCMP investigations? We were told, in answer to our questions on the floor of the House of Commons, not to worry, that we should have confidence that the Government will clamp down on those people and bring them to justice. What justice has there been in coming to grips with the abuse? The fact is that it is business as usual.
Those sleazy consultants, who make huge immoral profits from people like those we have met in our constituency offices who have paid thousands of dollars for nothing, are still in business. Even though they were raided by the RCMP they do not have to appear in court or face penalties.
These operators moved their tricks of the trade from Portugal to Turkey after we put a visa on Portugal, and moved to Brazil after we put a visa on Turkey. Now they have gone elsewhere. The people in communities in Toronto know who they are. Members of the same community provided evidence to government Members and the Minister at the Committee.
The Government knows the identity of those operators but there has been no action. If the Government is genuinely interested in stamping out abuse, why has not one person been fined or jailed in the last three years in light of the numerous schemes and scams in this country? Why has it not declared war on those white-collar criminals who live off the proceeds of human desperation? The Government must answer those questions because its policy is predicated on stamping out abuse.
We are asked to trust the Government, yet it has failed to come to grips with the situation. I challenge the Government to show me proof that it is serious about clamping down on abuse. If the Government is serious about stamping out abuse, why is it that not one person who has gone through the determination process and been refused a claim been removed

We had a boatload of refugee claimants in 1986. What was the response of the Government? The then Minister gave them ministerial permits which allowed them to stay in Canada. We had a fairly quick processing. We had a Prime Minister who welcomed them. Our Prime Minister declared very proudly, and 1 was happy to hear him, in terms of the Tamil refugee claimants: "If we err, we will always err on the side of justice and on the side of compassion". We all remember those words. That was the summer of 1986.
In the summer of 1987, the same Prime Minister, probably before he even talked to his Minister of Immigration-he has not even seen one of these individuals, he has not even participated in debate and he called the emergency-said: "These people by and large are illegal aliens". He also said: "I am not going to be pushed around or kicked around by these people". That was the summer of 1987. The summer of 1986 was radically different.
No one is suggesting that this Government be pushed around. No one in this Parliament would subscribe to that. We are all proud of protecting our shores, our sovereignty and our independence. However, that does not mean the Government has to prove its macho image. It does not have to prove how strong it is after giving up to the United States on lumber and free trade. It does not have to prove how strong it is by pushing around a boatload of people looking for a home.
The real dichotomy I wanted to address is the confusion of the electorate who are asking what our policy is. In 1986, in a very ad hoc way, the Government accepts. In 1987 it rejects, fabricating a crisis and bringing Parliament back, giving the whole situation an unreal and very fictitious air.
Which is real, the Prime Minister declaring the aliens illegal back in June, or his speeches at the various ethno-cultural picnics this past summer where he talked about tolerance and
opening the door to immigration? Canadians want to know, and this Parliament should know, which is the policy of this Government and of this country. This is the confusion we have to address and eradicate. The Government has to be confident its policies are secure, that they have clarity and purpose, otherwise confidence will be undermined and mistrust will be the order of the day.
The first response of the Canadians to the boatload of 174 migrants just a few short months ago was not to call the police. It was not to call the immigration officer, nor to call the Coast Guard to remove these individuals. The very first act was of a Nova Scotian woman who offered the migrants on her lawn tea and cookies. That was the first Canadian response. The first natural reaction was to offer these people tea and cookies and, I believe, peanut butter and jelly sandwiches. Think of it, Mr. Speaker for a moment. We have gone from that natural and beautiful knee-jerk reaction of a Canadian woman, to Bill C-84, and we know what happened in between.
In terms of Bill C-84, we have to ask ourselves two questions, what and why. What is in Bill C-84, and why are those clauses drafted the way they are? Again, I preface my remarks by suggesting that if the objective of the exercise is to curb abuse, that is fair. If we wish to say that our country is open to asylum seekers and we wish to honour our obligations and responsibilities to legitimate refugees, but not to others, that is fair, legitimate and expected and no arguments will be offered from any quarter of this House. But does Bill C-84 do that? Who are the targets? That is why the Hon. Member for Spadina (Mr. Heap) and I, who attended those committees, moved the amendments. We tried to clarify the objectives with the reality, with the law. We tried to move amendments so that the Bill would actually do what the Government purports it will do.
I would like to take a moment to go over a number of the major clauses in the Bill. One clause heralded by the Government is that it gives new power to turn boats back. The Government wants to tell Canadians it is going to be tough, that it is going to put into its legislation the power to enable us to turn boats back. It expects applause for that bravado. But let us analyse what that will mean. What will that do to the process of our refugee system? How will you and I, Mr. Speaker, ever know who was on that boat? If that boat contained 100 passengers, how many were true refugees, 59, 73, 100 or none? How many had passports and proper visas, 6, 12, 14? What were their circumstances? Where were they coming from? What were they fleeing from? What were their circumstances in terms of the actual persecution they faced?
The answer, of course, is that we would not know. They would not be provided due process. There would be no hearing where they could go into details of their persecution. There would be total disrespect in this regard for any processing of that unknown passenger, and we may be participating in sending 100 persons, 15 or one person back to the country of origin to be tortured, to face imprisonment or to face death. 1

do not think Canadians really feel comfortable about that possibility.
The second aspect we have to analyse is that if the Government really wants to deter, is this the proper way to do it? Is it proper to simply say: "We are going to turn the boat around and that will end it"? Or do we need something else? I believe the latter. If I were a captain who was prepared to set sail from Europe, what would I be thinking if I knew the policy of Canada was simply to turn the boats around? I would do the following. Perhaps I would have room for 100 individuals. I would charge them each $10,000. I would pocket the money and 1 would say, "There is a 50 per cent chance that I am going to get in in the middle of the night, dump the passengers, return and perhaps fill up the boat again and go somewhere else or return to Canada. Or there is a 50 per cent chance that even if the Coast Guard finds me, the only thing that they will do, or the Minister will do, is simply to turn my boat around". Perhaps the captain of the boat will dump the passengers beyond the 12-mile limit. Perhaps he will dump them off in another country or bring them back to their country of origin. We must not forget that he has the money and the boat. He has made a profit. Thus the captain wins. He wins in all situations, whether or not he is turned back.
In an amendment we suggested that if there is a boat approaching our country that we board it and escort it into port, which will allow us to do two things. First, it will allow us to determine who the passengers are, whether or not they are refugees. If so, they will be determined as such, and if not, after processing, they will be asked to leave. Second, we will have the captain's boat. We can impound it or sell it. We can charge the captain or fine him. We can imprison the captain. In answer to those who suggest that it is not the captain who is the real organizer but someone else in another country, let me say that we can use the evidence that we obtain from the captain and the crew to try to track down that operator, smuggler number one, and use any powers that we have to extradite him or, through the use of pacts with other countries, ensure that we bring to justice those who are smuggling.
If one really wanted to deter the captain of a boat from leaving that European harbour, would it not make sense to try to approach it and escort it into port rather than turning it around, remaining ignorant of who is on board, who did the organizing and where these people come from? Ignorance and political darkness do not help us define what we are trying to stop. That is why we moved an amendment which would provide for escorting a boat into port rather than turning it around at sea. That would not discourage any captain or smuggler. It does not offer process. So we lose and we come up with a fat zero in terms of processing and in terms of dissuading people from smuggling.
The other factor, of course, is that it would create two types of refugee claimants. It would allow the person who comes in other than on a boat to have a processing system while those

who arrive by boat may not have one. For example, if my family were fleeing a country facing political persecution and I left by boat and my brother left by plane, my brother would arrive through Pearson International Airport, declare his refugee status and would have a hearing. He would be processed and he could stay. Since I came by boat I could be turned away and I would not be able to tell my story. There is one policy which creates two classes of refugees.
As a policy we cannot suggest that it is the mode of transportation which will dictate the decision-making process. One cannot say, "If you take a bus, we will process you this way. If you take a plane, we will do it this way. If you take a boat, we will do it another way". There has to be one system for each refugee claimant. A person is either a refugee or not. Either the country provides processing or it does not. If we create two different types of refugees and a person wants to come here and abuse the system, do Hon. Members not think that those people will now take a plane rather than a boat until we deal with all transportation vehicles in the same way if we wish to curb abuse? I think it would be logical. Again, an amendment by my Party to achieve that end was defeated.
The third aspect of this point is this. What about the Geneva Convention and our international obligations? At the outset of my remarks I mentioned the two responsibilities that we enjoy as a country under the United Nations Convention. There is the policy of non-refoulement which is a very classy technical word which simply means that we will not send people back to a place unless we can guarantee or be certain that it will not be problematic, hazardous or fatal for that person. That is clear. The policy of turning back a boat will not guarantee the process of non-refoulement. So we would be violating very seriously that responsibility.
We asked the Government, "If you no longer believe in the conventions of the United Nations, if you do not believe in the agreement we signed in 1951, then tell Canadians that you want to break that agreement and that you want another configuration, that you do not believe in it any more, that you are going to go your own way". At least the Government should have the courage of its convictions to tell Canadians clearly and to allow Canadians to judge for themselves whether or not they would like to pull out of this United Nations pact. The Government should not do that in a backhanded way by trying to insert a clause in a piece of legislation which will do that very thing.
With respect to turning back boats, we moved amendments that would in fact curb real abuse while protecting the rights of claimants to tell their stories. That was rejected.
Another proposal in the Bill suggests that travel companies have to play the role of immigration officers. It is suggested that travel companies in Canada must confiscate all travel documents, all visas and all passports from incoming passengers. The representatives of companies who testified before the committee said that this proposal is unworkable. They said

that they do not have the ability legally to confiscate documents belonging not only to a person but to the country of that person's origin. They argued with respect to liability, for example, if passports or visas are stolen, lost or misplaced. Whose responsibility would that be? Would it be the responsibility of the Canadian Government or of air transportation companies such as Air Canada or Air France?
They talked about the possibility of terrorist activities. They said that if there were a terrorist on board who wished to terrorize an individual of a certain denomination, sect or religion, it would be easy for such an individual to get a stewardess and go through all the documents in order to identify by picture the individuals belonging to that creed or denomination. They did not want to elicit or encourage terrorists by making life easier for those individuals who want to bring harm to passengers on board an airplane. They also talked about the inconvenience of collecting and then redistributing at the end of flights passports and other travel documents. The other message was that all passengers would run the risk of losing their documents for a period of time, including Canadians coming back to this country, unless there was an exception, and there was not.
Therefore, Canadians must ask themselves what kind of regulation would require the confiscation of all documents on airlines coming into Canada. Not even the Soviet Union or Iron Curtain countries ask that of their national airlines. Canadians and witnesses asked us as members of the committee, "Do you want to legislate that type of legislation which would place us in a very unique class all our own? Or do you want to set a standard of which we can be proud and try to work to curb abuse without infringing upon our values, our temperament, our way of doing things in this country?" The Government refused. It persisted and said, "No, all passengers, Canadians and non-Canadians, will have their passports confiscated. Airlines will be fined". The airlines are not paying fines now. I doubt that even Air Canada will pay fines, and it is the national airline owned by the Government which would actually fine its own airline, which probably would not pay. Is that a logical, workable policy? Are we to be proud of that policy? I think not.
Another area is the powers to detain individuals. My colleagues and I do not argue with the fact that if a person comes to Canada without identification, without proper documentation, does not co-operate, and perhaps there is information that that person is possibly a threat to this country, of course all Canadians would want the country to protect itself and assure its citizens that there is due regard for that potential threat. That is why in the present system there are automatic detainment powers for 48 hours. A Minister or officials can detain a person for 48 hours. After that time there can be an application to an adjudicator who, based on further evidence and information, can allow a further detainment of seven days which would follow for every seven-day period.
That was passed by a former Parliament, and approved by the government Members who were then in opposition. It also met with the approval of Canadians who felt it was a good compromise to allow for the detainment powers and for the adjudicator to make the decision on whether there is proper evidence, not only suspicion, to detain a person. We are not only talking about the infringement of rights of potential new arrivals, but of the possible infringement of the rights of other Canadians and the manner in which the courts interpret them.
The Charter clearly specifies that no Canadian will be detained unreasonably without proper grounds and without a process where an adjudicator makes the determination. If the Government provides the adjudicator with well-founded reasons, evidence, and documentation, the adjudicator says, yes, we will detain. If the Government has a hunch or a suspicion that that person is an undesirable, that hunch or suspicion is not good enough in this country. No one would want to be locked up on a hunch or a suspicion.
Therefore, we suggested that the current law was adequate. It was doing the job. There were no problems. If there was evidence, there was a detainment. The Government proposes in Bill C-84 an automatic detainment of seven days, rather than the 48 hour detainment. After seven days, there can be an additional 21 day detainment without the adjudicator being in a position to say yes or no. The adjudicator would merely stamp the approval, because there is no flexibility in the Bill. There is no discretion that the adjudicator may not grant the detainment. The legislation clearly states that the adjudicator "shall" offer his or her approval. We must underline the word "shall". The adjudicator is a rubber stamp. In that case, I do not know why there would be an adjudicator. It gives excessive powers that the Government on a whim, a hunch, or a suspicion can detain a person for 28 days with no questions asked, no representation, no legal remedies, nothing.
1 am suggesting that this is an infringement on those rights, and it is an infringement of the Charter. It is an infringement on Canadians' sense of justice and fair play. If detainment is needed, it can be granted, but it cannot be granted on a hunch or a suspicion. It will be a sad day if we allow this proposal to go through unchallenged. It will end up in the courts. Legal experts and witnesses have suggested that it will be challenged in the courts because it contravenes the Charter of Rights and Freedoms. Of course, if this clause is challenged together with other clauses, the Bill will be dragged through the courts. It will die a slow and agonizing death. Perhaps in a year or two we will have a policy that is paralysed. Then what will the Government tell Canadians? Will it say, "We were in a rush. We thought we could have done it. We now find out that the Supreme Court has said no. We have to return to the drawing board"? Is that the manner in which the Government should proceed?
If there is a hunch or a suspicion that a person may be an undesirable, there is the possibility of making a determination that that person should not enter the refugee process. That is very dangerous. What information will be relied upon? If
