Nelson Mandela arrived here, and the Government had information that he is considered an undesirable in South Africa, or was in prison in South Africa, which would therefore make him a criminal under South African law, and he is accused of the crime of standing up for human rights and democracy, does that mean that that information will be used against an individual? There is not one international code of law. That is the reason people flee and become refugees. A person standing up for democracy in Chile may be thrown in prison. A person standing up for democracy in Canada may be elected as a Member of Parliament. That information, and that recognition of our law compared to other laws has to be taken into account. The Government would rely on information provided by the government of a country from which that person is fleeing in order to fabricate an undesirable clause.
I am suggesting that this is not the manner in which to proceed. If there is information provided by that government or country, the refugee body should be allowed to make a determination. The commissioners can decide that the information is faulty and in fact that it proves that the person is a political refugee, or the refugee commissioner can say that the information is legitimate and it should be used against the person. We must allow the person the discretion to defend himself from information from a country or a government which states that he or she is guilty of a crime, which crime may have been to stand up for democracy, or to throw a rock through someone's office window.
We received enlightened testimony with respect to those excessive over-kill powers in this clause. Mr. Borovoy, the Chairman of the Canadian Civil Liberties Association, stated:
It is a violation of democratic principle to create a power of jailing people- on the basis of a unilateral, essentially unreviewable decision of a politician . . . consider the incongruity this creates with our criminal law.
He went on to say:
The powers created by this Bill are excessive, repressive, and needless. No less gratuitous is the rush to get it enacted yesterday.
If the Canadian Civil Liberties Association is suggesting that this measure is repressive, why is the Government moving ahead? If the Canadian Civil Liberties Association and the Canadian Bar Association say that this will be challenged in the courts, why is the Government moving ahead? If the Government wishes to respect the reality of people who are fleeing and who are charged with so-called crimes because they wish to be free and have human dignity, why is this reason for detainment or refusal into the system? Is that not the reason that we have a refugee process? Are refugees not extradicted from their country because they cannot be free, they do not have freedom of choice, speech, assembly, all the things that we have in our Constitution? That is the very same Constitution that we patriated only a few short years ago. We brought it home and created a Charter of Rights and Freedoms that is the envy of the world.
We made amendments to clarify, refine, target, and bring it in line with our justice system. A right infringed upon today

with respect to the 174 migrants is a right that infringes upon all of us. That is the manner in which to look at human rights.
The fourth area of concern is the powers given to immigration officers for the first time. On a whim or a suspicion they can kick down the doors or jump through the windows of any organization and seize any document without a warrant. They do not even need a tele-warrant, which is used when the officer concerned cannot get to a judge and so makes the request by telephone. These officers do not need to do even that. No warrants at all are required. We are going to have immigration officers playing Rambo on suspicion.
We in this Party said that at the very least the Government must accept the need for a mandatory warrant. The only exception would be when someone's life is in danger. Other than that, should we allow immigration officers to break down doors at whim? Will Canadians accept that? Or do Canadians accept that there should be checks and balances so that a warrant is required? That is what Canadians voted for in the past. That is why we have a Charter of Rights. We are protected from search and seizure without a warrant. Why should immigration officers be given the power to ransack a place because they have a hunch that a particular person is not a refugee? As the Canadian Civil Liberties Association said, it goes far beyond what is needed.
The Canadian Bar Association and professors of constitutional law have said that if this legislation is passed, it will be challenged in the courts. It will be eaten up by the courts. It will render our policy unworkable. Therefore, why do it? Requiring a search warrant is reasonable, moderate, in keeping with Canada's sense of justice, yet the Government turned it down.
The fifth area of great concern is that of proposed Sections 95.1 and 95.2. Those sections epitomize the over-kill this Bill represents. According to those sections, any Canadian, whether a priest, a nun, a student or a farmer, who assists a refugee who may not have a document in his pocket showing he is a legitimate refugee, is liable to a fine or imprisonment. Imagine that. We are passing a law that would allow a priest to be imprisoned or fined for helping a refugee. What is the role of churches and non-governmental organizations? What has their role been in the food banks of this country? I do not think there is anything more embarrassing and undignifying for a human being than having to line up to ask for food. Imagine your feelings if you were in that position. What has been the reaction of the churches to the poor, those who do not have clothing, the homeless, those who are addicted to drugs or who are involved in prostitution? The reaction has been to try to complement government action in a humanitarian and compassionate way. We accept that. What would be the price if we did not have that network of volunteers? Yet now, all of a sudden, the church or individual who helps a refugee is liable to a fine or imprisonment. That is repugnant.

Is that the kind of law we want? Is it the kind of law we should be proud of? Or should we recognize that the action of a priest in helping a refugee is different from the action of a smuggler, a manipulator, or a consultant who trafficks in human beings for profit? The target should be those who circumvent our laws for profit. The churches came before the committee and said they have never, ever counselled fraudulent claims. They never tried to suggest to claimants that they rip up their documents. They never suggested that claimants arrive in the middle of the night. The Ministers responsible have said for two weeks now, "Do not worry, Member of Parliament for York West, we made the law such that it will get the real smugglers. Do not worry, our intentions are not to imprison or fine a priest or the organization involved".
If those are their intentions, why are their intentions not reflected in the law? If those are the speeches, why are they not the law of the country? You cannot say that the intention is not to fine a priest while at the same time you provide a law that allows a priest to be fined. It is either one or the other, Mr. Speaker. This country is not governed by speeches or intentions, it is governed by law. This law will create a new offence which is not there now. In 1987 or in any other year we cannot be proud of finding in our legislation a Bill that can fine and imprison individual Canadians who legitimately help refugees. What kind of a country do we want to become? Do we want to be like the United States where priests have to hide refugees in basements? Do we want to make the actions of a priest acts of civil disobedience? Are we suggesting that a priest who helps a refugee is a potential criminal, as that sort of law would imply if he were caught and charged? I do not think Canadians want that. They did not want it this summer, they did not want it 10 summers ago, and they will not want it in 10 years to come.
We tried to move an amendment to suggest that it should not be a crime for a priest to help a refugee but that it should be a crime to counsel fraudulent claims, to suggest tearing up documents, to smuggle people for profit and dump them in the seas. Let us fine people and put them in prison if we have to, but let us not create a law that suggests that we make the net so large and so encompassing that we can catch everybody potentially under the law. Again, intentions are one thing and laws are different. Intentions are useless when the law allows you to prosecute individual innocent Canadians.
With respect to the clause, we had a very moving brief presented by the Inter-Church Committee on Refugees. I would like to select what two individuals said. First, George Cram said:
In our opinion Bill C-84 does not help the process.
I do not want to be guilty of committing an offence for doing humanitarian work. 1 do not want to feel inside myself that what I am doing is illegal, and 1 do not want to be liable for prosecution. The offence is what you are creating, not the prosecution.
With him was Nancy Pocock, a member of the same InterChurch Committee, who said:
If my Government tells me it is a crime to help these people, I will have to say I am obeying a higher law and I am going to continue to help them when they need me.

We tried to suggest to the Government that there are words and clauses that one can use in the legislation under the law to distinguish very clearly between the act of a consultant or a smuggler and the Nancy Pococks and George Crams of Canada. We suggested the words "non-profit", "voluntary", "humanitarian", which have been used 38 different times in our federal statutes. What about the definition of churches? This was not only to make the intention known but to allow these individual Canadians not to have their legal rights infringed upon and not to lose their civil liberties for assisting people they had been assisting for years. Those phrases were all possible. We have the best legal minds in the Justice Department, I would think, or at least access to the best legal minds, and yet we were unable to get from the Government agreement to amend proposed Sections 95.1 and 95.2 to state clearly that it is not the law in Canada to allow for prosecution of individuals who aid, abet or assist a refugee without a visa.
Government members were stubborn and inflexible, and the Minister, in his final address to the committee, has stubbornly refused to heed all the witnesses who had cited proposed Sections 95.1 and 95.2. They said, "For goodness' sake, clean it up. Amend it. Make it clear in law that we are not your targets". Those sections are on the record, on the books, and they are about to become law. If Canada has been a leader in the international community, as it has, this will allow the Great Britains, the Switzerland and the United States of the world to say that if Canada can do it, we can do it. What are the two most important responsibilities with which we in this Chamber are entrusted? The first is to ensure that Canadians' tax dollars are spent wisely and prudently. The second responsibility is to draft the laws of the country, to create laws that will govern and administer the citizens of the land.

In this case, the Canadian Bar Association has said that every junior lawyer could take a shot at this Bill. The Civil

Many of my constituents are hoping that we finally come up with a system that works, but they do not want to see a policy that does not work two years down the road. What will we do then; call back Parliament again for another summer? Two summers in a row we have been here for emergencies. Every summer there is an emergency. If it is really an emergency, we should do it right.
There is an onus on the Government and on Members of Parliament to deal swiftly with abuse, to ensure that we target the real abusers. However, we should not pass into law the clauses for which I have concern and then allow those clauses to be subjected to the courts. The courts will say: "What kind of legislation is this? Why did you create a Charter of Rights in 1981 if you wanted to abuse it in 1987?"
It is very discouraging and disheartening that the Government has not listened, that it has not allowed the input of Members, churches, legal experts, civil libertarian groups and members of the Canadian Bar Associations who want to work with the Government to ensure that this is a good piece of legislation. Civil liberties groups do not have vested interests in putting down a policy for the sake of putting it down. They do not want to threaten or suggest that if a policy is not successful they will be heroes. These groups are interested in legislation which will work. Canadians have those interests as well, but they have not been listened to or heard.
Canada is a very privileged country. It is a great nation by all estimations. It is a tolerant and compassionate country. I do not think any Canadian would trade his or her place with anyone in any other country. Although the United States of America is our friend and ally and is more powerful and perhaps richer in certain respects, I do not think we would trade places with an American on any day of the week.
As my Leader has suggested quite articulately on many occasions, there is a price to be paid for being a Canadian, but it is a price worth paying. We do not mind paying that price for being a Canadian, enjoying the fruits of this country, and ensuring a certain type of life for our families and others who wish to come here.
I think we all aspire to make our country bigger and better. We should not rest on our laurels or those of former Governments which did noble things or enacted progressive legislation. We should always strive, whether in government or other spheres, to improve and to enjoy a lifestyle and reputation which is the envy of the world.
Canadians want to take our place in the international community in a forceful way. We believe that we have the dynamism, youth and vigour that goes with a youthful nation and the independence and ability to strive for an influential place in the world. We could be a moderating force on the international stage. Canada is not isolated from the world in a vacuum. When Canada speaks, we want other countries to have respect for our country, our Prime Minister and our institutions. That is the third characteristic of being a citizen of this country.
We have had that role with regard to the refugee policy which we are discussing. We have been a leader on the international stage. The people of Canada received the Nansen Medal. It was the first time that the Nansen Medal for assistance to refugees was awarded to a people rather than a person. That is international leadership and international respect. That is salesmanship of our country abroad.
We live in a global community. We interact, communicate and influence each other with every act and every word. The Nansen Medal speaks for our country. We are proud when we go abroad-

Thank you very much, Mr. Speaker. I do not think the House Leader of the NDP deserves an answer because that was an improper question. The Parliamentary Secretary is following the hypocritical tendencies of the Government which tries to deal with two Bills at the same time. He will pay the price and not Canadians. I had wanted to complete my remarks before six o'clock and I hope, notwithstanding the interventions of the NDP and the Parliamentary Secretary, that I will. If I do not, I do not.
I was speaking about the three characteristics of our citizenship and perhaps nationhood. The first one was with regard to the greatness of our country, the second was with regard to the desire to build it bigger and better and to improve it, and the third was with regard to our desire for a role of influence and respect in the international community. The fourth point is that we are a society which bases itself on orderly systems of procedure and the premise that our rules and laws should be respected.
I believe that while it is legitimate to cut out abuse and keep from our borders those who wish to smuggle in other human beings, that desire is not incompatible with the four characteristics which should clothe our citizenship. Helping refugees and attaining the other three characteristics does not detract from each other.
Immigration Act, 1976
The only real solution to this problem is for the Government to get moving on a new refugee system which would recognize the transition of which I spoke earlier in my remarks. That is the only solution. We have had three years of inaction by the Government which has ignored the requests, pleas, suggestions, reports, commissions, studies, media, facts and figures. It is time that the Government made it a priority. That is what Canadians are demanding and that is what we, as the Opposition, are trying to ensure.
While we may lose every vote and every amendment, I do not think our arguments will be lost on the country. The debate we are trying to encourage throughout the country concerns the value of our amendments and our words.
While the Parliamentary Secretary and others on the government side may be smug in knowing that they have the numbers, the more important question concerns the attitude and the vision of this country. Canadians will not pay attention to whether Motion No. 4 lost or Motion No. 8 won; they will be looking at who speaks for them and for the type of country to which they want to belong. Is it the person who advocates making it illegal for a priest to help a refugee, or the person and the Party who supports that action as a noble one which has been part of our society for years? Will they support the Member who wants to turn away the boat without due process for the passengers, sending them back to probable death or persecution, or will their support go to the Member who would escort the boat back to port and allow the passengers to disembark so that we may know the stranger, look him in the eyes and make a determination while, at the same time, find the captain who dumped 174 people in the ocean at two in the morning and put him in prison if necessary? Which Member will Canadians listen to?
Is it the Member who suggests that immigration officers should play Rambo and break into church organizations without warrants, or the Member and Party that advocates that if there is reason to search and seize and there is a warrant, we should do so. If human life or safety is in danger, then it is not necessary to have a warrant. If it is not possible to get a typewritten warrant, then use the tele-warrant.
Which Member and Party will Canadians listen to? Is it the Party that advocates that all documents be confiscated on the airlines, putting us in a class not even equalled by the Soviet Union, or the Party that believes airlines should not confiscate all passports and documents? It is not right to remove the documents of a Canadian who returns from Florida after the winter. There must be another way.
Will Canadians listen to the Party that suggests people should be locked up for 28 days on a hunch, with no questions, or the Party that believes that if there is a substantial basis, proper documentation, and the adjudicator has numerous reasons for detainment, then there should be detainment?

September 2, 1987

The issue is not a question of Motion No. 4 versus Motion No. 8 and the fact that Liberals lost the amendments. It may warm the hearts of government Members that the Liberals presented 20 amendments and not one of them passed. Liberal Members may say they are depressed that they lost all 20 amendments. Neither reaction presents the real story. The real story is the vision of Canada that those amendments embodied. The real story is how legislation approved in this Chamber affects Canada, our people and our society.
Whether the legislation involves refugees, budgets, tax reforms, senior citizens or the Meech Lake Accord, the question is: how does it affect the lives of Canadians in our ridings and those wishing to come to our shores?
Is there not a responsibility for immigrants who are now Canadian citizens not to close the door after coming to Canada? Would 1 be responsible in suggesting that now that I am in Canada and enjoy the privileges of my society we should close the doors out of some fear?
We are not talking about abuse, because abuse should be eliminated in a very forceful way. However, under the laws and provisions of our Constitution, do those of us who are immigrants really want to close the doors behind us? Rather, as a privileged society in the world, should we not say that we cannot close the door? It was open when 1 came, there were regulations that 1 met, why cannot those same regulations apply to strangers wishing to come to our shore?
Is there not a price worth paying to be Canadian? Would you not rather live in a country that understood a refugee as a person who goes through disorder? There is a concept that the system would work better as a neat, tidy little package in which crystal-clear decisions can be made within two or three weeks. But what is the world of a refugee? It is one of disorder, disunity and cloudiness. They have no home or orientation. A refugee's world is one of fear and apprehension.
While we must have a system that curbs abuse and accepts legitimate refugees, we cannot believe that the system will be foolproof, tight, and inflexible. Perhaps that is a price we pay as Canadians.
Perhaps those of us who were born here and have the privilege and rights of citizenship in this country should imagine that we were born in another time or another place in the middle of a war or during strife. What would we do to come to this country?
Who are refugees? Do we make it a crime if someone does not have a document when he arrives? Should we not allow that person to explain why he or she fled without a document? Is it a crime for a priest to help a refugee who does not have a document? According to the Civil Liberties Association, someone who kills, rapes and steals in broad daylight has more rights than those afforded to a claimant under Bill C-84. Is that balanced and proper? Is that acceptable? I do not think it is.
The intention of the law should be to discourage those who wish to abuse the system and allow a fair processing for those who wish to enter and apply for refugee status.
I began my speech by quoting Gunther Plaut who suggested that we should not forget about these strangers because at one time we were all strangers. Perhaps that is the way I will close the remarks at third reading.
To be a Canadian means many things to many people. To be a new Canadian means to have been a stranger, to have come from the old to the new, to have left the familiar for the unfamiliar. Those of us, particularly we legislators, who deny the stranger also deny Canada and its future.
I would like simply to close my remarks with the hope that the Government will change its mind at the eleventh hour and modify some of the clauses in Bill C-84, or at the very least accept a sunset clause. If this legislation is an emergency, let us treat it as an emergency. Emergency by its very definition does not last forever. Emergencies are temporary. They are short term. Why should we have emergency legislation become permanent legislation? Why not have this emergency legislation specific and fixed, but when we deal with Bill C-55 and the real solution, Bill C-84 should become redundant, null and void. At the very least, I appeal to the definition of "emergency", temporary, short term and short lived. There is no reason we should have these legislative scars on the books of our laws. They should be stricken from the laws of a progressive Canadian society in 1987.
Perhaps the challenge is that we look at it in terms of the year 2000. What do we think now of the actions of a former Government which, in 1939, turned away the boat called the St. Louis carrying 900 Jews who were escaping the horrors which faced them in their countries? How does the Government's actions in 1939 stack up against this Government's actions in 1987? I think the first reaction must be to ask, why? Why would a government turn away a boatload of 900 Jews, most of whom never saw the light of day after they touched the shores from whence they came?
These 900 people could have made their homes in Canada. Some of them might have become Members of Parliament. Others could have been teachers, judges or scholars. They were denied that opportunity. We can make up for the actions of the Government in 1939 and live up to the expectations of those who will replace us here in the year 2000, so that they can be proud of the compassion demonstrated by the Government and the Parliament during the summer of 1987.
Let us not be the Government which is the architect of a piece of legislation about which in the year 2000 and beyond, the then Member for York West will rise and ask how the Government in 1987 ever passed Bill C-84? Let us find a better place for ourselves and for our country in the annals of history.

1 simply want to conclude with the following comments of Rabbi Gunther Plaut to the committee:
I think that Draconian and emergency legislation gives the wrong signal, not only to the world but it gives the wrong word to our own people in Canada.
I think the Bill was drawn in undue haste. This is why I think we need just a little more leisure to write legislation that makes sense.
He then pleaded with the committee saying:
I ask you to look carefully at some of the amendments suggested. Do not follow the worst instincts of people, follow the best instincts.
If we follow the best instincts of Canadians, their aspirations, feelings and their desire for our nation, we will not go wrong and the world will not get the wrong message. If we follow the worst instincts, we will pay a bigger price and that price will bring us shame.
